newsitem.title: GERMANY: German unemployment has peaked - Labour Office Chief.
newsitem.headline: German unemployment has peaked - Labour Office Chief.

text.p: Germany's unemployment has peaked and is likely to average just under 4.3 million in 1997 but it remains unclear if and how soon the situation will improve, Federal Labour Office President Bernhard Jagoda was quoted as saying on Wednesday.

Jagoda told Die Welt newspaper in an interview that the decline in west German unemployment in June was better than usual for that month and said he firmly believed more people would find work from September at the latest.

"We are seeing first signs of a stabilisation... If I take everything into account I come to the conclusion that we've reached the trough. Whether and how quickly the upturn will come remains open," Jagoda said.
He added it was no surprise the economic recovery was failing to spur job creation because productivity gains were outstripping growth in gross domestic product.
Jagoda said the economy creates 150,000 jobs with every percentage point by which economic growth exceeds productivity growth.
"From that one can see that economic revival alone is not enough to reduce unemployment quickly," he said.
Germany's jobs market was hampered by a complex set of structural problems for which there was no single all-encompassing solution, Jagoda said.
"We need a reduction in the public share of the economy, deregulation, innovations, a reduction in overtime, flexible working hours. But it's not enough to talk about it. We need to act."
All sectors of the economy needed to step up innovation.

"At present we achieve our export successes mainly with mature products of medium to high levels of technology. But German companies are less represented in areas of top technology and in markets with good growth opportunities. We are obstructing job opportunities."
